source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
finding: Incubation has a small positive average effect on problem solving, but results vary a lot across studies.
numbers: 117 studies, 3,606 participants, median 25 per study. Weighted mean unbiased d = 0.29, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.39. Unweighted mean 0.41 (CI 0.28 to 0.54). 85 studies had positive effects. Cochran Q = 173.99, df 113, p < .001. Between-study variance .0834.
limits: Mostly small-sample studies. Large heterogeneity means the mean hides cases with no effect (e.g. Olton & Johnson 1976).
agent_relevance: Baseline claim: a break helps a little on average, not reliably. Supports keeping incubation out of the schema as a core operator.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (publication bias check)
finding: The authors checked for publication bias, found none, and did not correct for it.
numbers: Regression of effect size on sample size: standardized beta = .08, p = .41 (funnel plot judged symmetric).
limits: A regression test has low power with heterogeneous designs. The unconscious-thought literature (b17) shows such tests can miss bias.
agent_relevance: Do not over-trust d = 0.29; it may be inflated by small studies.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (cognitive load of break task)
finding: Breaks filled with an undemanding task gave larger effects than demanding tasks; rest sat in between.
numbers: Table 4 subgroup means: high-load task k=76, d about 0.24; low-load task k=22, d about 0.52; rest k=16, d about 0.46. Regression: low load beat rest only for linguistic problems (beta = .54, p < .05).
limits: Table text was garbled in extraction, so subgroup means are read from the printed table row. Only 16 rest and 22 low-load studies. Low-load edge over rest was specific to linguistic problems.
agent_relevance: Demanding interleaved work (tool-heavy sub-tasks) between attempts would be the analog of a high-load break and is predicted to help least.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (preparation and problem type)
finding: Longer preparation before the break gave bigger incubation effects. Visual insight problems benefited less than creative and linguistic ones when no cues were present.
numbers: Preparation length: positive significant regression coefficient. Problem-type subgroups: linguistic k=65, visual k=35, creative k=14.
limits: Moderators are correlated across studies (not randomized), so causal reading is weak.
agent_relevance: Incubation-like pauses only make sense after a real, long first attempt (impasse), echoing the stage model's preparation stage.

source: Wagner, Gais, Haider, Verleger & Born (2004) Sleep inspires insight
finding: After training on a number-reduction task, sleep roughly doubled the chance of finding a hidden shortcut rule compared with staying awake.
numbers: Main experiment: 13 of 22 (59.1%) gained insight after night sleep vs 5 of 22 (22.7%) in each wake group; chi2 = 8.54, df 2, P = .014. 66 participants (age 18-31). Control without initial training: 25% insight in two conditions.
quote: more than twice as many subjects gained insight into the hidden rule
limits: Small groups (about 22 each). One task. Sleep vs wake is confounded with time of day in the main design. 5 early solvers were replaced.
agent_relevance: The founding sleep result. The effect acts on implicitly encoded structure, which has no clean LLM analog without weight updates.

source: Lacaux et al. (2021) Sleep onset is a creative sweet spot (Science Advances)
finding: A conceptual extension of Wagner's paradigm found that a minute or so of light sleep (N1) tripled insight, while deeper sleep (N2) removed the effect.
numbers: N = 103, 20 min break. Insight 83.3% (20 of 24) in N1, 30.6% (15 of 49) in wake, 14.3% (2 of 14) in N2. Across groups Fisher P < .001; wake vs N2 P = .32. 16 who solved before the break were excluded.
limits: Group membership depends on who falls asleep, so it is not randomized. Small N2 group (14).
agent_relevance: Sleep effect depends on depth. Which stage matters is contested (see b07).

source: Loewe, Petzka, Tzegka & Schuck (2024) Sleep inspires insight: a preregistered study (CCN)
finding: A preregistered conceptual replication of Lacaux found no N1 effect but an N2 effect, the opposite of Lacaux on N2.
numbers: N = 90 did a 20 min nap; 68 analysed. Insight 85.7% (24/28) N2, 63.6% (14/22) N1, 55.5% (10/18) wake. Earlier no-nap baseline 48.5% (48/99); with nap 70.6% (48/68), Fisher p = .007. Steeper EEG 1/f slope predicted insight beyond sleep stage (AIC 81.15 vs 82.5).
limits: Different task (perceptual decision task with a hidden colour rule). Conference paper. N1 vs wake did not differ.
agent_relevance: Two labs, two tasks, opposite verdicts on N2. The sleep-insight link is task and stage dependent, not a stable law.

source: Schoenauer et al. (2018) Sleep does not promote solving classical insight problems and magic tricks (Front Hum Neurosci)
finding: A 2x2 design (3 h sleep vs wake, incubation vs none) found no benefit of sleep or incubation on classic insight problems or magic tricks.
numbers: N = 77. Magic tricks: incubation F(1,64) = 0.008, p = .930; sleep F(1,64) = 0.047, p = .829. Extra tricks solved: s_inc+ 1.35, s_inc- 1.47, w_inc+ 1.42, w_inc- 1.35. 54% of solutions came with insight. Insight-solved tricks: incubation F(1,46) = 2.305, p = .136 (numerical only).
limits: Daytime sleep averaged 121-133 min with only 10-17 min REM. Small cells (15-19). Tasks need restructuring, not remote association.
agent_relevance: A failed replication on hard restructuring tasks. Incubation may help association-type tasks more than representation change.

source: Sanders, Osburn, Paller & Beeman (2019) Targeted memory reactivation during sleep improves next-day problem solving (Psych Sci)
finding: Replaying sounds tied to unsolved puzzles during slow-wave sleep raised next-morning solving of those puzzles.
numbers: N = 57. Solved 31.7% (SD 28.3) of cued puzzles vs 20.5% (SD 18.9) of uncued; t(56) = 3.22, p = .002, dz = 0.47 (55% relative gain). Cued solving correlated with cued memory r(55) = .37, p = .004. Memory for cued and uncued sound-puzzle pairs was equal (70.3% vs 73.5%).
limits: Within-subject; one lab; no independent replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Strongest causal sleep evidence: cue the unsolved problem during sleep. Analog: reinsert the open problem into a later context.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving
finding: Review of three accounts of incubation: unconscious work, intermittent conscious work, beneficial forgetting. The author favours unconscious work.
numbers: Cites Strick et al. 2011 (92 decision studies, g = 0.224 for immediate incubation) and Sio & Ormerod (117 studies, mean d = 0.29).
limits: Review by an advocate of unconscious work. The large replication in b17 undercuts the decision-making part.
agent_relevance: Gives the map of rival mechanisms; discriminating tests are in b11 to b15.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving, reporting Baird et al. (2012) thought monitoring
finding: Rules out intermittent conscious work: the number of task-related thoughts during the break did not predict later performance.
numbers: As summarised: frequency of target-related intermittent thoughts during incubation was unrelated to later performance (Baird et al. 2012). Author concludes it is safe to rule out intermittent work.
limits: Thought reports are self-reports and may miss brief covert thoughts.
agent_relevance: If true, a pause helps for reasons other than hidden continued thinking; hard to copy in an LLM.

source: Segal (2004) Incubation in insight problem solving, as reported in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Fresh-look account: any switch away after impasse helps, whatever the break task and its length.
numbers: Spatial parallelogram-in-square problem; after impasse 4 or 12 min of crossword or newspaper browsing, then up to 6 more min. Break beat no break; no effect of break length or task demand.
limits: Secondhand via Gilhooly. Conflicts with Sio & Ormerod's finding that low-demand tasks beat demanding ones; one problem only.
agent_relevance: Suggests the ingredient is leaving a stuck state, which an agent can mimic by resetting context.

source: Smith (1995) Beneficial forgetting, as reported in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: With misleading cues, participants solved more when they had forgotten the cue, and forgetting grew with break length.
numbers: As summarised: word problems with helpful or misleading cues; various break lengths; solving higher when the misleading cue was forgotten.
limits: Secondhand. Cannot explain immediate-incubation effects, where no time passes to forget.
agent_relevance: Maps to dropping a failed plan from context before a retry.

source: Gilhooly et al. (2013) similarity of break and target task, as reported in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: A discriminating test: a break task in a different modality helped divergent thinking more than a similar one, opposite to what beneficial forgetting predicts.
numbers: Verbal anagram vs spatial rotation break tasks crossed with verbal (alternate uses) and spatial (mental synthesis) divergent tasks; significant incubation effects plus a cross-over interaction.
limits: Secondhand. Divergent tasks, not insight problems.
agent_relevance: Evidence for some non-conscious work; no clear LLM analog.

source: Baird, Smallwood, Mrazek, Kam, Franklin & Schooler (2012) Inspired by distraction: mind wandering facilitates creative incubation (Psych Sci)
finding: A break with an undemanding task, which let minds wander, improved later creative uses on the same problems. Demanding task, rest or no break did not.
numbers: N = 145. Exposure x incubation interaction F(1,141) = 4.98, p < .01. Repeated-exposure problems: incubation effect F(1,144) = 4.99, p < .01; undemanding beat demanding, rest and no break (all p < .01). Rest vs no break p = .30; demanding vs no break p = .35. New problems: no effect (p = .39). Mind wandering higher in the undemanding task (M = 2.47 vs 2.15, p < .05).
limits: Divergent task (Unusual Uses), not insight. Rest alone gave no benefit. Effect only on previously seen problems.
agent_relevance: The break benefits problems already seen. A break that loads new unrelated content may still work if it is undemanding.

source: Cai, Mednick, Harrison, Kanady & Mednick (2009) REM, not incubation, improves creativity by priming associative networks (PNAS)
finding: In a nap study with Remote Associates items, REM sleep improved integration of unassociated information more than quiet rest or non-REM sleep.
numbers: Abstract-level only: REM nap vs quiet rest and NREM; benefit not explained by memory of primes. No exact numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened; numbers missing. Schoenauer et al. (b08) had little REM and no effect.
agent_relevance: Association priming during sleep; relevant only to association tasks.

source: Nieuwenstein, Wierenga, Morey, Wicherts, Blom, Wagenmakers & van Rijn (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage (JDM)
finding: A large replication of the 'distraction beats deliberation' decision effect found nothing, and a bias-corrected meta-analysis gave about zero.
numbers: N = 399 (within-subject). Accuracy: deliberation male 50.8%, female 61.7%; distraction male 55.4%, female 65.1%; mode of thought Wald chi2 = 1.09, p = .30. Power .997 at d = .218. Meta-analysis pooled g = 0.15 (CI .03 to .26, p = .01); after trim-and-fill g = 0.018 (CI -.10 to .14, p = .77).
limits: Decision-making paradigm, not insight problems. Bayes-factor value not read cleanly this session.
agent_relevance: Immediate-incubation effects in choice tasks look small or absent. Treat unconscious-work claims with care.

source: Nieuwenstein et al. (2015), reliability vs moderator accounts
finding: The replication met every moderator condition the earlier meta-analysis said makes the effect strong, and still found no effect. Significant studies were confined to small samples.
numbers: Strick et al. 2011 moderators (global mindset, short deliberation) were met. The six earlier positive studies gave d = .69 as the H1 prior; replication power .999 at that size.
limits: Does not disprove incubation for insight problems; targets the choice paradigm.
agent_relevance: Warning: moderator stories that rescue small-sample effects often fail under a large test.

source: Strick et al. (2011) unconscious-thought meta-analysis, as reported in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: 92 decision studies gave a small beneficial aggregate effect of immediate incubation, bigger with more options, shorter presentation and a global mindset.
numbers: g = 0.224 (as reported by Gilhooly).
limits: Secondhand. Revised down to g = 0.018 after bias correction in b17.
agent_relevance: Do not cite g = 0.224 without the later correction.

source: Dijksterhuis & Meurs (2006), as reported in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Responses to a brick-uses task were more creative when a short distracting task came right after the instruction.
numbers: Reported as better creativity than control. Gilhooly notes the instructions did not ask for unusual uses.
limits: Secondhand. Gilhooly et al. 2012, with standard instructions, found the immediate benefit larger than the delayed one.
agent_relevance: Immediate incubation is the cleanest break analog, but its replication record is mixed.

source: Schoenauer et al. (2018), classic insight problems
finding: For matchstick, nine-dot and eight-coin problems, retest gains were similar across sleep and wake groups.
numbers: Retest solving: nine-dot sleep+incubation 36.8% vs wake+incubation 26.3%; eight-coin 21.1% vs 42.1%; matchstick 66.7% vs 90.9%. Initial solving 45.5% matchstick, 6.0% nine-dot, 8.0% eight-coin.
limits: Cells of about 15-19, wide standard errors, wake sometimes numerically ahead. Retest gain is confounded with practice.
agent_relevance: Practice alone raised solving. Any agent retry gain needs a no-pause control.

source: Schoenauer et al. (2018), discussion of moderators
finding: Authors argue incubation helps association tasks like the RAT through spreading activation, but not tasks that need a changed problem representation.
numbers: Cites Segal 2004, Bowden 2005, Vul & Pashler 2007 and Weisberg 2015 as studies with null or partial incubation effects.
limits: Authors' interpretation, not tested directly.
agent_relevance: If restructuring is the bottleneck for an LLM, a pause will not fix it; it needs a changed frame (an operator), not time.

source: Kumar, Vincentius, Jordan & Anderson (2025) Human creativity in the age of LLMs (CHI)
finding: Randomized experiments with LLM help: assisted rounds were better, but later unassisted performance did not gain and ideas became more alike.
numbers: About 1,100 participants in two experiments. Originality across conditions H(2) = 9.14, p = .010 (post hoc p = .009 vs no-LLM). Fluency H(2) = 8.57, p = .014.
limits: About humans using LLMs, not LLMs incubating. Not an incubation study.
agent_relevance: No carry-over from outside help; scaffold design should not rely on temporary crutches.

source: Nair, Gizzi & Sinapov (2024) Creative problem solving in large language and vision models: what would it take?
finding: A position paper that maps the four-stage creativity model to LLM pipelines: preparation to problem formulation, incubation and illumination to knowledge representation and manipulation, verification to evaluation.
numbers: Reports preliminary experiments; no incubation-specific effect measured.
limits: No incubation manipulation; the mapping is conceptual. Cites Helie & Sun 2010 and Gizzi et al. 2022.
agent_relevance: The stage model has been used as an LLM design frame without any test of the incubation stage.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models
finding: Mid-chain 'Aha' shifts in reasoning models are rare and usually go with lower accuracy, not insight.
numbers: 1M+ traces, three domains. Shifts in about 6.31% of traces; accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces. Formal detector fires on 1.79% of samples.
limits: Qwen2.5 and Llama GRPO runs plus some API models. A shift is defined by surface cues, not by human-style insight.
agent_relevance: An LLM analog of illumination does not help by itself.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026), entropy-gated intervention
finding: Triggering a reconsideration cue only when token entropy is high reliably improved accuracy across domains.
numbers: Entropy-gated second pass (top 20% entropy): +8.41 percentage points on MATH-500; smaller gains on crosswords and Rush Hour.
limits: Needs logit access; gains reported on small models.
agent_relevance: A measured way to add a re-look step: gate it on uncertainty, not on time.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: On riddles that need a representation shift, LLMs do far worse than humans; models often generate the right answer and then do not endorse it.
numbers: 38 frontier LLMs, 201 riddles. Non-reasoning models average 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%, humans about 53% (52.9%, CI 46.6 to 59.2) on a 120-item subset. English thinking beat Japanese thinking in one model comparison (p = .0071).
limits: Language-specific puzzles; model and human prompts differ. Thought-log analysis is exploratory.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is verification, not generation. This favours stronger verification operators over an incubation step.

source: Cordi & Rasch (2021), Brodt et al. (2018), as cited in Loewe et al. (2024)
finding: The preregistered replication paper states that several studies found no sleep benefit for insight, or none beyond awake rest.
numbers: Named null or mixed studies: Cordi & Rasch 2021; Schoenauer et al. 2018; Brodt et al. 2018.
limits: Only as listed in a conference paper; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: The weight of evidence for sleep and insight is mixed, not a clean win for Wagner.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving (CLARION), as cited in Nair et al. (2024)
finding: A computational model (CLARION, explicit-implicit interaction) implements the four stages: preparation, incubation, illumination, verification.
numbers: No numbers in the citing text.
limits: Not opened; fits to human data not read.
agent_relevance: The only model-level treatment of incubation met in the LLM-adjacent literature this session.

source: Search note: LLM incubation studies
finding: Searches this session found no LLM study that manipulates an incubation break and measures solving. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited.
numbers: Zero direct tests found. Adjacent: b23 (Kumar), b24 (Nair), b25-b26 (illusion of insight), b27 (NazoNazo).
limits: Absence of evidence given a limited search and blocked APIs.
agent_relevance: No empirical case for adding an incubation operator; consistent with schema section 4b.
